camps.name: Wallace Creek basin ridge camp
camps.why: The usual camp at the highest trees, about 5,700 to 6,000 ft, within reach of the couloir for a 2 AM start; you carry the full pack up the old road bed and brush to get here.

camps.name: Middle Fork Nooksack road switchbacks
camps.why: A car-side sleep before the walk-in, not a night of the climb itself; it buys an early start on the road switchbacks and costs a very long day-one carry.

camps.name: East Rankin Lake
camps.why: The lower stopping place at 5,120 ft; fine after a late start or a washed-out road, but it leaves a longer, higher summit day than the ridge camp.

camps.name: Saddle tarns above Rankin Creek
camps.why: A small stop between the lake and the ridge camp; it trims little from summit day, so most parties continue to the trees above.

camps.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
camps.why: The only practical camp: flat spots on the south shoulder above the glacier, about 4,800 to 5,000 ft, with a short glacier approach to the climb and no developed sites, so camp on durable ground.

new_camps.name: Green Creek Glacier south shoulder camp
new_camps.why: The established spot for this basin: flat ground on the south shoulder above the glacier base, about 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and close to the Cinderella col approach.
new_camps.notes: Reached after a five-mile, 4,000 ft approach from the Elbow Lake trailhead, including a Middle Fork Nooksack crossing. There are no developed sites, so use low-impact ground.

camps.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
camps.why: The only practical camp: flat spots on the south shoulder above the glacier, about 4,800 to 5,000 ft, with a short glacier approach to the climb and no developed sites, so camp on durable ground.

camps.name: Boulder Ridge high camp
camps.why: The usual camp where the ridge path meets the glacier, about 5,500 to 5,700 ft; windy and exposed, but it keeps the summit day to a long but manageable push.

camps.name: Boulder Ridge high camp
camps.why: The usual camp where the ridge path meets the glacier, about 5,500 to 5,700 ft; windy and exposed, but it keeps the summit day to a long but manageable push.

camps.name: Hogsback Camp
camps.why: The plan's staging camp via the Heliotrope Ridge trail, about 6,000 ft on the moraine beside the Coleman Glacier; running water in season, no trees, and the shortest approach to the ridge.

camps.name: Park Glacier camp near the Portals
camps.why: The camp for parties who come in from Artist Point along Ptarmigan Ridge; snowmelt only for water, and it is a separate, longer approach than this plan describes.

camps.name: Camp Kiser, Ptarmigan Ridge
camps.why: The first night on the Ptarmigan Ridge approach from Artist Point, where the maintained trail ends; not used on the Heliotrope Ridge approach this plan follows.

plan_conflict: Camps on file put most parties at the Portals via Ptarmigan Ridge, but the plan approaches by Heliotrope Ridge to the Hogsback; no trip report on the Cockscomb itself was found to say which is right.

camps.name: Hogsback Camp
camps.why: The standard camp, about 6,000 ft on the moraine beside the Coleman Glacier, with running water in season; above the trees so no food hang, but it is the closest sleep to the glacier.

camps.name: Kulshan Cabin site
camps.why: A lower fallback at about 5,000 ft with trees for shelter and a toilet; it leaves another thousand feet of climbing on summit morning.

camps.name: North Ridge glacier bivy, upper Coleman
camps.why: A snow camp around 6,700 to 7,000 ft on the Coleman Glacier, as the plan calls for; it shortens the walk to the headwall base but is fully exposed and sited by crevasse conditions.

camps.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge
camps.why: The usual lower staging camp at about 6,000 ft with running water; parties wanting an easier carry sleep here and take a longer glacier walk on summit morning.

camps.name: Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
camps.why: Sheltered sites at 4,800 to 5,000 ft with trees and toilets; useful after a late start but a much longer summit morning.

camps.name: Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes
camps.why: A higher snow camp near 7,000 ft that cuts summit day further; exposed to wind and dependent on the year's crevasse pattern.

camps.name: Colfax-Grant saddle bivy
camps.why: A very high, fully exposed saddle used mainly as an emergency stop after weather or a slow descent, not a planned night on a two-day trip.

plan_conflict: The file lists two mains; the plan puts camp at about 6,700 ft on the glacier, so the glacier bivy is the main, and the Hogsback is demoted to an alternative. Only one older report on the headwall itself was found.

new_camps.name: Hogsback Camp
new_camps.why: The standard camp for the Coleman-Deming, on the moraine at the edge of the glacier, so skis go on right from camp; no trees, but streams run nearby in season.
new_camps.water: Meltwater streams run through camp in season; treat before drinking.
new_camps.capacity: Party size is limited to 12 people.
new_camps.permit: A recreation pass is required at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
new_camps.notes: About 2.9 miles and 2,200 ft from the trailhead via Trail 677. Above treeline, so use a bear canister or Ursack and pack out waste unless at the toilets lower down.

camps.name: Sandy Camp, top of the Railroad Grade
camps.why: The common camp at about 6,000 ft at the top of the grade, with water nearby and a short summit approach; it fills up in summer, so arrive early for a flat site.

camps.name: Railroad Grade and Morovitz Meadow camps
camps.why: Lower sites for a late start or a slower pace; they are drier and add several hundred feet of climbing to summit day.

camps.name: Hogsback
camps.why: The standard staging camp at about 6,000 ft by the Coleman Glacier; the summit day returns here, and it has running water in season but no trees for hanging food.

plan_conflict: Night 2 is spent back at the Hogsback after the summit day; the plan's day 3 is the walk out.

camps.name: Park Glacier camp near the Portals
camps.why: A sheltered, sandy site at the Portals where most parties sleep before the headwall; snowmelt is the only water, and it puts the climb close to camp.

camps.name: Camp Kiser, Ptarmigan Ridge
camps.why: About five miles out Ptarmigan Ridge where the trail ends; a shorter first day for a three-day trip, but it leaves the glacier crossing for the next morning.

camps.name: Crag View Camp
camps.why: The camp for this route, about 6,500 to 6,800 ft between the Easton and Squak glaciers, with open tent sites and running water nearby in season; the climb starts from the doorstep.

camps.name: Middle Blum Lake
camps.why: A short step above the lower lake at about 5,000 ft; the summit day starts from here, but sites sit on heather and slab and it catches more wind.

camps.name: Lower Blum Lake
camps.why: The common base at 4,900 ft just above the brush; a little lower and more sheltered, with a slightly longer start to the climb.

camps.name: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
camps.why: Only for a party caught by dark on the steep forest climb; no flat ground or water, so it is a forced stop, not a plan.

camps.name: Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
camps.why: The highest practical ground at 5,700 ft; it trims summit day but costs a final carry after the brutal approach, so few sleep here.

plan_conflict: The file marks both Middle and Lower Blum Lake as main; research supports the lakes as one base, so Middle is kept as the main and Lower becomes an alternative.
